pos: n. (Jacobus Arminius, 1560–1609, Dutch minister and professor at Leiden whose teaching on conditional election provoked the controversy settled at Dort)
etymology: Latinized form of Dutch Jakob Harmenszoon; Jacobus, from Hebrew Ya'aqob, supplanter.
biblical_def: Jacobus Arminius was orphaned young, educated at Marburg, Leiden and Geneva under Beza, and settled as a preacher in Amsterdam before his 1603 appointment to the chair of theology at Leiden. He was by all accounts an able and gracious man; the dictionary does not quarrel with his manners but with his doctrine. Asked to refute a tract against predestination, he came instead to doubt the Reformed position, and taught that election is God's decree to save those whom He foresees will believe, that the atonement is universal in its intent, and that grace, though necessary, may be finally resisted. Each of those propositions reverses the direction of Scripture's own sentences. Rom 9:16 settles the question of origin: “So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.” Act 13:48 settles the order: “as many as were ordained to eternal life believed.” John 6:44 settles the ability: “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him.” Arminius died in 1609 before the storm broke; his followers drew up the Remonstrance the next year, and the Synod of Dort answered it in 1619.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines election as the choice of one or more from a greater number; and in theology, divine choice, or predetermination of God, by which persons are distinguished as objects of mercy.
webster_full: ELEC'TION, n. The act of choosing; choice; the act of selecting one or more from others.
ELEC'TION, n. In theology, divine choice; predetermination of God, by which persons are distinguished as objects of mercy, become subjects of grace, are sanctified and prepared for heaven.
ARMIN'IAN, a. Pertaining to Arminius, or designating his principles.
scriptures: Rom 9:16
So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.
And when the Gentiles heard this, they were glad, and glorified the word of the Lord: and as many as were ordained to eternal life believed.
John 6:44
No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.
Eph 1:4
According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:
corruption_summary: Arminianism is not a milder Calvinism but a different account of who saves whom; Dort answered it point for point and the answer still stands.
corruption_paragraphs: The error at the root is a reversal of order. Scripture makes faith the fruit of election; Arminius made election the acknowledgement of foreseen faith. Act 13:48 puts the ordaining first and the believing second, and Eph 1:4 puts the choosing before the foundation of the world, which is before there was any foreseen anything. Once the order is reversed the whole chain in Rom 8:30 loosens, for a predestination that waits upon man's decision cannot guarantee the calling, the justifying or the glorifying that the verse strings to it.

Modern evangelicalism has largely absorbed the Remonstrant position without knowing its name, and preaches a love of God that waits at the door of a will it dare not enter. That is not generosity toward sinners; it is a smaller gospel, because it leaves the decisive act in the hands of the dead. John 6:44 is the plain refutation: the Father draws, or no man comes. The Reformed answer honours God's mercy precisely by refusing to make it conditional upon the creature.
roots_summary: Greek eklegomai (G1586), to choose out; horizo (G3724), to mark out; helkuo (G1670), to draw.
roots_lines: Greek eklegomai (G1586) — to choose out for oneself; Ephesians 1:4.
Greek tasso (G5021) — to appoint, to ordain; Acts 13:48.
Greek helkuo (G1670) — to draw, to drag; John 6:44.
Greek eleeo (G1653) — to show mercy; Romans 9:16.
Greek proorizo (G4309) — to predestinate; Romans 8:30.
usage: “it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth” (Rom 9:16) — the will is not the origin.
“as many as were ordained to eternal life believed” (Act 13:48) — the ordaining comes first.
“No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (John 6:44) — the drawing is decisive.

pos: n. (Simon Episcopius, 1583–1643, Dutch Remonstrant theologian, spokesman for the Arminian party at the Synod of Dort)
etymology: Latinized from Dutch Bisschop, bishop; Simon, from Hebrew Shim'on, hearing.
biblical_def: Simon Episcopius succeeded Arminius as the ablest mind of the Remonstrant party and led its delegation to the Synod of Dort in 1618. He was a student of Arminius at Leiden, a professor there from 1612, and a controversialist of genuine power. At Dort he refused to be examined as a defendant and insisted on arguing as an equal party; when the synod would not grant it, he and his colleagues were expelled from the assembly and afterwards banished from the United Provinces. In exile he wrote the Remonstrant confession of 1621 and organized the party into a church. His later theology moved further than Arminius had, loosening the doctrine of the Trinity's necessity for salvation and treating many settled articles as matters of liberty. That drift is the standing evidence that the Remonstrant principle does not stay where it is first set down. Jude 1:3 names the obligation he set aside: believers are to “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.” Tit 1:9 names the qualification he inverted, that an elder hold fast the faithful word “that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a remonstrance as a strong representation of reasons against a measure; and heterodox, as contrary to the doctrines of Scripture, or to the received doctrines of the church.
webster_full: REMON'STRANCE, n. Show; discovery. A strong representation of reasons against a measure, either public or private.
HET'ERODOX, a. Contrary to the faith and doctrines of the Scriptures; contrary to the received or established doctrines of the church.
TOLERA'TION, n. The act of tolerating; allowance given to that which is not wholly approved.
scriptures: Jude 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.

They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us: but they went out, that they might be made manifest that they were not all of us.
corruption_summary: Episcopius proved by his own career that a confession held loosely at one point will be held loosely at the next.
corruption_paragraphs: The Remonstrant case was pleaded as a plea for moderation, and moderation is how every loosening of a confession is pleaded. But 2Ti 1:13 does not commend a loose grip: it commands believers to “Hold fast the form of sound words.” The form is a shape, not a mood, and the holding is firm, not tentative. Episcopius began by asking liberty on the five articles and ended by extending liberty over articles the whole church had held from Nicaea. The trajectory is the argument.

The modern form of this is the plea that doctrinal precision is divisive and that the generous church should hold its confession as a historic document rather than a binding standard. Tit 1:9 forecloses it: the elder is qualified by holding fast, and the purpose clause is to convince the gainsayers, which is impossible for a man who has conceded that there is no settled word to convince them with. 1Jn 2:19 gives the sober outcome of such departures, that they go out from us because they were not of us.
roots_summary: Greek epagonizomai (G1864), to contend earnestly; antecho (G472), to hold fast; hupotuposis (G5296), a pattern.
roots_lines: Greek epagonizomai (G1864) — to contend earnestly about a thing; Jude 1:3.
Greek hupotuposis (G5296) — an outline, a pattern, a form; 2 Timothy 1:13.
Greek antecho (G472) — to hold firmly to; Titus 1:9.
Greek antilego (G483) — to gainsay, to contradict; Titus 1:9.
Greek paradidomi (G3860) — to deliver over, to hand down; Jude 1:3.

“Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13) — a shape, firmly held.
“both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9) — the eldership's polemical duty.

pos: n. (Johannes Bogerman, 1576–1637, Frisian minister, president of the Synod of Dort, principal translator of the Dutch Statenvertaling)
etymology: Dutch surname; Johannes, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious.
biblical_def: Johannes Bogerman presided over the Synod of Dort from November 1618 to May 1619 and is remembered chiefly for the session in which he dismissed the Remonstrant delegation with a torrent of words that even his friends thought intemperate. The judgement on his temper should not obscure the judgement on his work. Under his chairmanship the synod produced the Canons of Dort, the most careful corporate statement the Reformed churches ever made on the doctrines of grace, framed not as a party manifesto but as a point-by-point answer to the five articles of the Remonstrance. Bogerman then gave the rest of his life to a greater labour still: with Willem Baudartius and Gerson Bucerus he translated the whole Bible into Dutch from the original tongues, the Statenvertaling of 1637, which did for the Netherlands what the Authorized Version did for England. Isa 55:11 is the promise such work rests upon, that God's word “shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please.” Psa 68:11 describes the result: “The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a synod as an ecclesiastical council; a meeting of ministers and other delegates to consult on matters of religion; and a version as a translation from one language into another.
webster_full: SYN'OD, n. A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion.
VER'SION, n. A translation; the act of translating; the rendering of thoughts or ideas from one language into another.
PRES'IDENT, n. An officer appointed or elected to preside over a corporation, company or assembly.
scriptures: So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
corruption_summary: A synod's canons and a nation's Bible came out of the same decade and the same conviction, that the word of God must be both guarded and given.
corruption_paragraphs: It is worth noticing what Dort did with its victory. It did not content itself with condemning error; it set the Scriptures into the hands of ploughmen in their own tongue. The two acts belong together. Act 17:11 commends the Bereans because they “searched the scriptures daily” to test what they had heard, and a people cannot do that in a language they do not read. Confessional precision without a vernacular Bible breeds a clergy-kept faith, and a vernacular Bible without confessional precision breeds a thousand private religions.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What it faces is neglect. The principle to recover is that the church's doctrinal standards and the church's Bible translation are one work, undertaken by the same men in the same fear of God, and that 2Ti 3:16 makes the inspired text, not the committee, the final authority which the committee exists only to confess.
roots_summary: Hebrew dabar (H1697), word; Greek anakrino (G350), to examine; theopneustos (G2315), God-breathed.
roots_lines: Hebrew dabar (H1697) — a word, a matter; Isaiah 55:11.
Hebrew 'emer (H562) — a saying, a word; Psalm 68:11.
Greek anakrino (G350) — to examine, to sift; Acts 17:11.
Greek theopneustos (G2315) — God-breathed, inspired of God; 2 Timothy 3:16.
Hebrew basar (H1319) — to bear tidings, to publish; Psalm 68:11.

“great was the company of those that published it” (Psa 68:11) — the Statenvertaling's company.
“All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) — the authority a synod only confesses.

pos: n. (Petrus Plancius, 1552–1622, Flemish Reformed minister at Amsterdam, cartographer and astronomer, a leading Counter-Remonstrant)
etymology: Latinized from Flemish Platevoet; Petrus, from Greek Petros, a stone.
biblical_def: Petrus Plancius fled the Spanish persecution in Brussels disguised as a soldier and settled at Amsterdam, where he served as a minister for thirty-seven years and became the sharpest of the Counter-Remonstrant preachers. He was also, improbably, one of the great cartographers of the age: he drew the charts that carried the first Dutch fleets to the East Indies, taught navigation to their pilots, named constellations of the southern sky, and argued for a northern passage to Asia. The two vocations were one in his mind. He pressed the Dutch East India Company to carry ministers with its merchants, and the earliest Reformed missions in the Indies grew from his insistence. Psa 2:8 was his kind of text: “Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession.” So was Mar 16:15, “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.” He opposed Arminius at every turn, and lived to see Dort vindicate the doctrine he had defended.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chart as a hydrographical or marine map, for the use of navigators; and to navigate, as to pass on water in ships.
webster_full: CH'ART, n. A hydrographical or marine map; a draught or projection of some part of the earth's superficies on paper, with the coasts, isles, rocks, banks, channels, and the like.
NAV'IGATE, v.i. To pass on water in ships; to sail.
COS'MOGRAPHY, n. A description of the world or universe.
scriptures: Psa 2:8
Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession.
And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
Psa 96:3
Declare his glory among the heathen, his wonders among all people.
Act 1:8

But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.
corruption_summary: The man who charted the sea lanes wanted ministers on the ships, which is the right order of priorities for any commerce.
corruption_paragraphs: Plancius is a rebuke to the modern separation of callings. He did not treat cartography as a secular trade pursued alongside a sacred ministry; he drew the maps so that the gospel could travel the routes. Act 1:8 sets the geography of the church's obligation, extending “unto the uttermost part of the earth,” and a man who knows where the uttermost parts are has an advantage in obeying it. Christian engagement with trade, science and navigation is not a distraction from missions; mishandled it becomes one, but rightly handled it is the road.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Psa 96:3 commands the declaring of God's glory “among the heathen” as a positive duty laid on the church, and that merchants, sailors and mapmakers in a Christian nation are under it as much as ministers. The Dutch companies largely failed at this; Plancius saw the failure coming and said so.

roots_lines: Hebrew goy (H1471) — a nation, the heathen; Psalm 2:8.
Hebrew 'erets (H776) — the earth, land; Psalm 2:8.
Hebrew caphar (H5608) — to recount, to declare; Psalm 96:3.
Greek ktisis (G2937) — creature, creation; Mark 16:15.
Greek eschatos (G2078) — uttermost, last; Acts 1:8.

“Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15) — the commission the fleets ignored.
“Declare his glory among the heathen” (Psa 96:3) — the duty of a trading nation.

pos: n. (Willem Teellinck, 1579–1629, minister at Middelburg, commonly called the father of the Dutch Second Reformation)
etymology: Dutch Teellinck, a Zeeland surname; Willem, Germanic, resolute protector.
biblical_def: Willem Teellinck was a lawyer's son studying for the bar when nine months among the Puritans of Banbury in England changed the course of his life. He saw there a household religion of family worship, Sabbath keeping, self-examination and practical godliness that the Dutch churches, orthodox in confession, largely lacked. He returned, took orders, and spent twenty-six years at Middelburg preaching and writing to bring that practical divinity home. He published some sixty works; The Path of True Godliness is the best known. The movement he began is called the Nadere Reformatie, the further or nearer Reformation, because its claim was that doctrine had been reformed while life had not. Jas 1:27 is its text in miniature, that pure religion is to visit the fatherless and widows and “to keep himself unspotted from the world.” So is 1Ti 4:16: “Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them.” Teellinck never set piety against doctrine; he insisted that a confession not worked into the conscience and the household is a confession not yet believed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines godliness as piety; belief in God, with reverence and obedience to His commands; and practical, as reducible to practice; capable of being used in practice.
webster_full: GOD'LINESS, n. Piety; belief in God, and reverence for his character and laws.
GOD'LINESS, n. A religious life; a careful observance of the laws of God and performance of religious duties.
PRAC'TICAL, a. Reducible to practice; capable of being used in practice, or applied to use.
scriptures: Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
1 Timothy 4:16
Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Mat 5:16
Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.
corruption_summary: A church may be confessionally sound and practically heathen; Teellinck said so to his own orthodox countrymen and was not thanked for it.
corruption_paragraphs: The Nadere Reformatie is sometimes mistaken for pietism, and the mistake matters. Pietism in its later German form tended to set the warmed heart against the defined creed; Teellinck set the warmed heart upon the defined creed and complained that his countrymen had the second without the first. 1Ti 4:16 keeps both in one sentence, the self and the doctrine, and promises the saving of hearers only to the man who continues in both. A ministry that drops either half has dropped the verse.

The live temptation today runs the other way from Teellinck's Holland. Where he faced sound doctrine without godliness, much of the modern church offers godliness-talk without sound doctrine, and calls it authenticity. Mat 5:16 ties the visible works to the Father's glory, not to the believer's reputation for sincerity; the good works are to be seen so that God is glorified. Teellinck's practical divinity was practical precisely because it was doctrinal first.
roots_lines: Greek threskeia (G2356) — religious worship, outward religion; James 1:27.
Greek aspilos (G784) — unspotted, free from blemish; James 1:27.
Greek epecho (G1907) — to hold fast, to give attention to; 1 Timothy 4:16.
Greek didaskalia (G1319) — doctrine, teaching; 1 Timothy 4:16.
Greek kalos (G2570) — good, beautiful, worthy; Matthew 5:16.
usage: “to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jas 1:27) — practical divinity in six words.
“Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine” (1 Timothy 4:16) — both halves, always.
“that they may see your good works” (Mat 5:16) — visible godliness, for God's glory.

pos: n. (Jodocus van Lodenstein, 1620–1677, minister at Utrecht, poet and hymnwriter of the Dutch Second Reformation)
biblical_def: Jodocus van Lodenstein studied Hebrew and Arabic under Voetius at Utrecht and served that city as minister from 1653 until his death. He is the man who gave the Dutch Second Reformation its name: in a 1674 work he spoke of a nadere reformatie, a further reformation, reaching from the church's doctrine into the church's manners. His preaching was searching to the point of severity, and his hymns, collected as the Uytspanningen, carried that searching note into Dutch homes for two centuries. He never left the established church, though he grieved over it, and he refused the separatist path that some of his admirers took. Psa 85:6 is the burden of his life's work: “Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?” Hab 3:2 is its prayer: “O LORD, revive thy work in the midst of the years.” He held that a reformation of doctrine which stops short of the conscience has reformed a library and not a people.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines revival as a renewed and more active attention to religion; and reformation, as change from worse to better; amendment of life.
webster_full: REVI'VAL, n. Return, recall or recovery to life from death or apparent death.
REVI'VAL, n. Renewed and more active attention to religion; an awakening of men to their spiritual concerns.
REFORMA'TION, n. Change from worse to better; amendment of life; correction of abuses.
scriptures: Psa 85:6
Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?
Hab 3:2
O LORD, I have heard thy speech, and was afraid: O LORD, revive thy work in the midst of the years, in the midst of the years make known; in wrath remember mercy.
Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
corruption_summary: He named the thing the Dutch churches needed and then stayed inside them to pray for it, which is harder than leaving.
corruption_paragraphs: Van Lodenstein's refusal to separate deserves attention, because the men who most sharply see a church's decline are most tempted to leave it. Heb 10:25 forbids forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, and the verse does not add an exception for assemblies we find cold. Reform from within is slower, costlier and less satisfying than departure, and it is ordinarily the duty. The conventicles he encouraged were supplements to the public worship, never substitutes for it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The temptation it names is perennial: to mistake disgust at a church's coldness for a call to abandon it. Hab 3:2 prays for revival within the years God has appointed, in the midst of them, and asks that in wrath He remember mercy. That is the posture of a man who knows the judgement is deserved and stays to intercede.
roots_summary: Hebrew chayah (H2421), to live, to revive; po'al (H6467), work; Greek episunagoge (G1997), assembling together.
roots_lines: Hebrew chayah (H2421) — to live, to keep alive, to revive; Psalm 85:6.
Hebrew po'al (H6467) — a deed, a work; Habakkuk 3:2.
Hebrew qerab (H7130) — the midst, the inward part; Habakkuk 3:2.
Greek episunagoge (G1997) — a gathering together, assembling; Hebrews 10:25.
Greek threskeia (G2356) — outward religious worship; James 1:27.
usage: “Wilt thou not revive us again” (Psa 85:6) — the Second Reformation's petition.
“revive thy work in the midst of the years” (Hab 3:2) — inside the church, not outside it.
“Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together” (Heb 10:25) — why he never separated.

pos: n. (Dutch, the Further Reformation; the movement for practical godliness in the Dutch Reformed churches, c. 1600–1750)
etymology: Dutch nadere, nearer, further; reformatie, reformation, from Latin reformatio.
biblical_def: The Nadere Reformatie was the Dutch answer to a question the Reformation left standing: what happens when a nation's churches are soundly confessional and its people are not converted. Beginning with Willem Teellinck and running through Voetius, van Lodenstein, Witsius and à Brakel, the movement pressed for family worship, strict Sabbath observance, self-examination, experiential preaching and church discipline that bit. Its name, coined by van Lodenstein, claims not a new reformation but a nearer one, carried further in from the pulpit toward the hearth. It took much from English Puritanism and gave much back, and its literature is among the richest practical divinity the Reformed churches have produced. Act 2:42 describes the pattern it sought to restore, a people who “continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.” 1Ti 4:16 states its method, taking heed to self and doctrine together. Its danger, which its best men saw, was introspection curdling into morbidity; its achievement was a generation taught to examine itself by Scripture rather than by feeling.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines piety as reverence of God and love of his character; and discipline, in ecclesiastical affairs, as the execution of the laws by which the church is governed.
webster_full: PI'ETY, n. Piety in principle, is a compound of veneration or reverence of the Supreme Being and love of his character.
DIS'CIPLINE, n. In ecclesiastical affairs, the execution of the laws by which the church is governed, and the infliction of the penalties enjoined against offenders.
EXPE'RIMENTAL, a. Known by experiment or experience; derived from experience.
scriptures: Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
1 Timothy 4:16
Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee.
Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
Psa 85:6
Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?
corruption_summary: A confession believed by the head and not the household is the condition the Nadere Reformatie existed to diagnose.
corruption_paragraphs: The movement's besetting danger was real and should be named. A preaching that endlessly tests the marks of grace can leave tender consciences unable ever to rest, and some Dutch congregations inherited a habit of perpetual self-inspection that kept believers from the Lord's Table for decades. The corrective is in the same Scriptures: Act 2:42 puts the breaking of bread among the ordinary continuing acts of the church, not among the rewards of attained assurance.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The modern misuse runs opposite: experiential preaching has been replaced by therapeutic preaching, which addresses the feelings without examining the heart and offers comfort without repentance. Psa 85:6 asks God to revive His people so that they may rejoice in Him, and the order there is not negotiable. The principle to recover is examination unto joy, not examination as a way of life.

Greek koinonia (G2842) — fellowship, communion; Acts 2:42.
Greek didaskalia (G1319) — doctrine, teaching; 1 Timothy 4:16.
Greek threskeia (G2356) — outward religious service; James 1:27.
Hebrew chayah (H2421) — to revive, to keep alive; Psalm 85:6.
usage: “continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship” (Act 2:42) — the pattern sought.
“Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine” (1 Timothy 4:16) — the movement's whole programme.
“that thy people may rejoice in thee” (Psa 85:6) — examination aimed at joy.

pos: n. (Adrianus Saravia, 1532–1613, Flemish-born divine, defender of episcopacy, one of the translators of the Authorized Version)
biblical_def: Adrianus Saravia was born at Hesdin of a Spanish father and Flemish mother, helped draft the Walloon Confession, fled to England, taught at Leiden, and ended as a prebendary of Canterbury and Westminster. He holds two distinctions that rarely meet in one man. He was among the earliest Protestant writers to argue that the Great Commission binds the church in every age and not merely the apostles, publishing in 1590 a treatise urging missionary obligation on churches that had assumed the commission expired; Beza wrote against him. And he was one of the Westminster company of translators for the Authorized Version of 1611. His defence of episcopal government put him at odds with the Presbyterians, and the dictionary does not follow him there, holding with the New Testament that elder and bishop name one office. Mat 28:19 is the text he recovered for the church: “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations.” Act 1:8 is its promised reach.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a commission as the act of committing, or a warrant or written letter conferring authority; and to translate, as to interpret; to render into another language.
webster_full: COMMIS'SION, n. The act of committing, doing, performing or perpetrating. A warrant or written letter conferring certain powers.
TRANSLA'TE, v.t. To interpret; to render into another language; to express the sense of one language in the words of another.
EP'ISCOPACY, n. Government of the church by bishops; that form of ecclesiastical government in which diocesan bishops are established.
scriptures: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
Act 1:8

But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.
And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!
corruption_summary: Saravia had to argue that the Great Commission had not expired, which tells you what the churches of 1590 assumed.
corruption_paragraphs: The Protestant scholastics of the late sixteenth century widely held that the apostolic commission died with the apostles, and so a century of Reformed churches sent almost no missionaries. Saravia saw the text would not bear it: the promise attached to Mat 28:19 runs to the end of the world, and a commission whose promise outlasts the apostles must itself outlast them. Rom 10:15 completes the argument, since preachers must be sent, and sending is the act of churches.

The error has a modern mirror in the claim that missions are a colonial imposition and that the churches of the West should now receive rather than send. The biblical answer is that sending and receiving are both commanded and neither is optional, and that Act 1:8 names a geography, not a direction of cultural traffic. Saravia's episcopal convictions, meanwhile, are to be rejected on the plain ground that the New Testament uses elder, bishop and pastor for one office.

“ye shall be witnesses unto me” (Act 1:8) — the reach of it.
“how shall they preach, except they be sent?” (Rom 10:15) — the duty of churches to send.

pos: n. (Johannes Althusius, 1563–1638, Reformed jurist and syndic of Emden, author of the Politica Methodice Digesta)
etymology: Latinized from German Althaus, old house; Johannes, from Hebrew Yochanan.
biblical_def: Johannes Althusius was a Calvinist lawyer who served as syndic of the East Frisian city of Emden for thirty-four years and wrote the most thoroughly Reformed political theory of his century. His Politica of 1603 builds the commonwealth upward from the family, the guild and the town rather than downward from the prince, treats every level of society as a covenanted association with its own God-given sphere, and lodges sovereignty in the people as a body under God, not in the magistrate. He defended the right of lesser magistrates to resist a tyrant, a doctrine with deep roots in the Reformed resistance writers. Later theorists of subsidiarity and federalism, including those who shaped the American constitutional order, drew from this well. Psa 127:1 governs the whole: “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it.” Rom 13 and Act 5:29 together set the limits, for the magistrate is God's minister and therefore not God, and “We ought to obey God rather than men.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a magistrate as a public civil officer, invested with the executive government of some branch of it; and a covenant, as a mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons.
webster_full: MAG'ISTRATE, n. A public civil officer, invested with the executive government or some branch of it.
COV'ENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act or thing; a contract; stipulation.
COMMON'WEALTH, n. An established form of government, or civil polity; a republic; a state.
scriptures: A Song of degrees for Solomon. Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Neh 4:14

And I looked, and rose up, and said unto the nobles, and to the rulers, and to the rest of the people, Be not ye afraid of them: remember the Lord, which is great and terrible, and fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses.
Psa 11:3
If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?
corruption_summary: Althusius built the state out of covenanted households rather than out of a sovereign's will, and the difference is the whole of political liberty.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors stand on either side of Althusius. On one hand the absolutist claim, revived in every age, that the state is the source of rights and the ultimate human authority; Act 5:29 denies it in six words, and the apostles said them to a lawful council. On the other hand the modern libertarian claim that the individual is the only real unit and every association is a voluntary contract between strangers; Neh 4:14 answers that by naming what men are to fight for — brethren, sons, daughters, wives and houses — which are the covenanted bonds Althusius made the state's foundation.

The contemporary corruption is the hollowing out of those intermediate bodies. Where family, congregation, guild and town are reduced to lifestyle preferences, nothing stands between the individual and the state, and the state expands to fill the vacancy. Psa 11:3 asks what the righteous can do if the foundations be destroyed, and the question is not rhetorical. The principle to recover is that God has ordained real authorities beneath the magistrate, and that defending them is a Christian political duty.

Greek peitharcheo (G3980) — to obey one in authority; Acts 5:29.

usage: “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it” (Psa 127:1) — the limit on all statecraft.
“We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — the magistrate is not final.
“fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters” (Neh 4:14) — what the commonwealth is made of.

pos: n. (Moïse Amyraut, 1596–1664, French Reformed theologian at Saumur, author of the hypothetical-universalist scheme named for him)
etymology: French; Amyraut, a Poitevin surname; Moïse, from Hebrew Mosheh, drawn out.
biblical_def: Moïse Amyraut was trained in law before John Cameron turned him to theology, and from 1633 he taught at the Protestant academy of Saumur. His Brief Traité de la Prédestination of 1634 proposed that God decreed to save all men conditionally upon faith, and then, foreseeing that none would believe, decreed absolutely to give faith to the elect. The scheme keeps unconditional election and effectual grace while making the atonement universal in intention. Three French national synods acquitted him of heresy; the Swiss answered him in the Helvetic Consensus Formula of 1675. The dictionary holds the scheme to be an error, not because its author was insincere but because its hypothetical first decree has no footing in Scripture. John 10:11 defines the atonement by its objects: the good shepherd “giveth his life for the sheep.” John 6:37 ties the giving and the coming into one chain. Amyraut's system posits a divine intention that never takes effect, which is a thing Scripture nowhere ascribes to God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines atonement as expiation; satisfaction or reparation made by giving an equivalent for an injury; and hypothetical, as including a supposition; conditional.
webster_full: ATO'NEMENT, n. Agreement; concord; reconciliation, after enmity or controversy.
ATO'NEMENT, n. Expiation; satisfaction or reparation made by giving an equivalent for an injury, or by doing or suffering that which is received in satisfaction for an offense.
HYPOTHET'ICAL, a. Including a supposition; conditional; assumed without proof.
scriptures: John 10:11
I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
John 6:37
All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.
Eph 1:4
According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:
Rom 8:30
Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified.
corruption_summary: Amyraldianism keeps every Reformed word and loosens the one joint that holds the atonement to the elect.
corruption_paragraphs: The decisive objection is not that Amyraut was too generous but that his first decree accomplishes nothing. Rom 8:30 runs predestination, calling, justification and glorification through the same company without loss, and a universal saving intention that saves nobody cannot be fitted anywhere into that chain. John 6:37 makes the Father's giving the ground of the sinner's coming, so that the extent of the Son's purchase and the extent of the Father's gift are the same extent.

The scheme is attractive today because it appears to let a preacher offer Christ sincerely to all without holding particular redemption. But the free offer never needed that help. Scripture commands the universal offer on the authority of the command, not on a universal intention in the decree, and the Reformed have always preached “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden” (Matthew 11:28) to every creature. Eph 1:4 locates the choosing before the foundation of the world and in Christ, which is where the atonement's extent is settled.

usage: “the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep” (John 10:11) — the atonement defined by its objects.
“All that the Father giveth me shall come to me” (John 6:37) — one company, one purchase.
“whom he did predestinate, them he also called” (Rom 8:30) — a chain with no slack in it.
